title: What did they say?
description: Lines you'll hear from servers, vendors, drivers, shop and hotel staff, in everyday polite Indonesian. Hear one, pick what it means, and learn a way to answer.

items.speaker: server
items.english: Eating here or taking away?
items.note: Dibungkus is wrapped to take away; the other answer is Dibungkus, ya.

items.speaker: server
items.english: What would you like to order?
items.note: Kak, from kakak (older sibling), is how staff address any young customer, man or woman.

items.speaker: server
items.english: And what would you like to drink?
items.note: Minumnya, 'the drink', comes once the food is ordered. The number goes after the drink, as with food.

items.speaker: server
items.english: How spicy would you like it? What level?
items.note: Places selling ayam geprek or spicy noodles rate the chilli by level, and level satu is already hot for most visitors. Level nol (zero) has none.

items.speaker: server
items.indonesian: Mohon maaf, nasi gorengnya sudah habis.
items.english: I'm sorry, we've run out of fried rice.

reply.indonesian: Oh, kalau begitu mi goreng saja.
reply.english: Oh, then I'll have fried noodles.

items.note: Habis means all gone. By evening, warungs often run out of the popular dishes.

items.speaker: server
items.english: Would you like more rice?

items.speaker: server
items.english: Anything else?
items.note: Sudah, 'that's it', is the usual answer; a bare tidak sounds abrupt.

items.speaker: server
items.indonesian: Mohon ditunggu, ya, Kak. Kira-kira lima belas menit.
items.english: Please wait. It'll be about fifteen minutes.
items.note: Mohon is the formal 'please' of staff and signs. When you ask for something, use tolong or bisa instead.

items.speaker: server
items.indonesian: Semuanya delapan puluh lima ribu, Kak.
items.english: That's eighty-five thousand altogether.
items.note: Prices are said in thousands of rupiah, and the word rupiah is usually left off.

items.speaker: clerk
items.english: Paying by cash or card?
items.note: Tunai is cash. Many staff just say cash, as in English.

items.speaker: clerk
items.english: Have you got anything smaller?

reply.indonesian: Maaf, tidak ada. Adanya seratus ribu.
reply.english: Sorry, no. I've only got a hundred thousand.

items.note: Uang kecil is small notes and coins. Small shops, stalls and drivers often can't change a big note.

items.speaker: clerk
items.english: Do you need a bag?

reply.english: No need, I've brought a bag.

items.speaker: clerk
items.english: Would you like to top up your phone credit while you're here?
items.note: Minimarket tills offer phone credit (pulsa) or the week's special with almost every sale. A smile and a no is fine.

items.speaker: vendor
items.english: What are you looking for?
items.note: Sellers call it out to passers-by. It's an invitation, not a question you need to answer in full.

items.speaker: vendor
items.english: That's already my lowest price.

reply.indonesian: Oh, ya sudah. Saya ambil satu.
reply.english: Oh, OK then. I'll take one.

items.note: Harga pas means the bargaining is over.

items.speaker: vendor
items.indonesian: Ya sudah, delapan puluh ribu boleh.
items.english: All right, eighty thousand it is.
items.note: Boleh here is the seller accepting your offer. Once they say yes, it's polite to buy.

items.speaker: vendor
items.indonesian: Mangganya manis, Kak. Mau coba dulu?
items.english: The mangoes are sweet. Want to try one first?
items.note: Fruit sellers often offer a taste. Boleh is the everyday yes to an offer.

items.speaker: driver
items.english: Going where it says in the app?
items.note: Sesuai means 'as per'. App drivers use it to check the destination as you set off.

items.speaker: driver
items.english: Where are you exactly?

reply.indonesian: Saya di depan pintu masuk, Pak.
reply.english: I'm in front of the entrance.

items.note: What drivers call or message to find you. Answer with a landmark.

items.speaker: driver
items.english: Here's your helmet.
items.note: Ojek drivers carry a helmet for the passenger, and wearing it is the law.

items.speaker: driver
items.indonesian: Lewat tol, ya, Kak? Lebih cepat.
items.english: Shall we take the toll road? It's quicker.
items.note: Toll fees are added to the fare, so taxi drivers ask first.

items.speaker: driver
items.english: Where would you like to be dropped off?

reply.english: In front of that mosque, please.

items.note: Turun is to get off or out: of a bike, a car or a bus.

items.speaker: receptionist
items.english: May I see your passport?
items.note: Literally 'may I borrow your passport'. Hotels copy the details, and it comes straight back.

items.speaker: receptionist
items.english: What name is the booking under?
items.note: Atas nama, 'in the name of', is for any booking.

items.speaker: receptionist
items.indonesian: Kamarnya di lantai dua, ya. Ini kuncinya.
items.english: Your room's on the first floor. Here's your key.
items.note: Indonesia counts the ground floor as lantai satu, so lantai dua is one floor up: what New Zealand calls the first floor.

items.speaker: receptionist
items.indonesian: Sarapannya mulai jam enam sampai jam sepuluh.
items.english: Breakfast is from six until ten.
items.note: Mulai … sampai … is 'from … until …', for any opening hours.

items.speaker: host
items.indonesian: Kamarnya belum siap, Kak. Mau titip tas dulu?
items.english: Your room isn't ready yet. Would you like to leave your bag with us?

items.speaker: receptionist
items.indonesian: Check-out jam dua belas siang, ya, Kak.
items.english: Check-out is at twelve noon.

reply.english: Could I make it one o'clock?

items.note: Check-in and check-out are said as in English.

items.speaker: host
items.english: Shall I book you a taxi?

reply.indonesian: Iya, boleh. Untuk jam tujuh pagi.
reply.english: Yes, please. For seven in the morning.

items.note: Dipesankan is pesan (to order) with di- and -kan: booked for you.

items.speaker: staff
items.indonesian: Silakan ambil nomor antrean dulu, Kak.
items.english: Please take a queue number first.

reply.english: Oh, where do I get one?

items.note: Banks, clinics and phone shops give out numbered tickets, and call the numbers out in Indonesian.
